title: Sounds and Me
summary: Read Finnish aloud, follow vowel harmony, use olla and your first verbs, ask and say no, count to 100, tell the time and introduce yourself.

lessons.title: Letters and sounds
lessons.objective: Read Finnish words aloud, including the letters ä, ö and y.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Finnish is read **as it is written**: one letter, one sound, and every letter is pronounced. The stress is always on the **first syllable**: `HEL-sin-ki`, `SUO-mi`. Learn the sounds once and you can read any word aloud.

cards.title: Three new vowels
head: Letter
Sounds like
Example
cards.body: These are separate letters, not a, o and u with decoration.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: `j` sounds like English **y**: `ja` (and) is said 'ya'. Finnish `y` is always a vowel. `h` is always pronounced, even in the middle of a word: `mehu` (juice). `r` is rolled with the tip of the tongue.

cards.title: Gliding vowels
cards.body: Two different vowels side by side glide into each other in one syllable: `ei` (no), `ai`, `oi`, `uo` in `Suomi`, `yö` in `yö` (night), `ie` in `tie` (road). These glides are called **diphthongs**.

cards.title: Dots matter
cards.body: `ä` and `a` are different letters that change the meaning: `sää` (weather) but `saa` (gets). In the same way `ö` is not `o`, and `y` is not `u`: `kyy` (viper) but `kuu` (moon). Always type the dots.

terms.say: Two different vowels said together in one syllable, gliding from one to the other, like ei or uo.

lessons.title: Long and short sounds
lessons.objective: Hear and write the difference between short and long vowels and consonants.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: In Finnish, **length changes meaning**. A double vowel (`uu`) is held about twice as long as a single one (`u`). A double consonant (`ll`, `kk`, `ss`) is held too. Write what you hear: one letter for a short sound, two letters for a long one.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A double consonant is a tiny stop: `kuk-ka`, `kis-sa`, `mat-to`. Your mouth closes, waits a moment, then opens. For a long vowel, just hold the sound: `tuu-li`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: English writes double letters without changing the sound (`apple`, `coffee`). In Finnish a double letter is always really long. Write `kisa` when you mean cat and you get 'contest'.

terms.say: Two of the same consonant in a row, like kk or ss. You hold the sound a moment longer.

lessons.title: Vowel harmony
lessons.objective: Pick the right ending (-ssa or -ssä, -ko or -kö) by looking at a word's vowels.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Finnish vowels form three groups. **Back vowels**: a, o, u. **Front vowels**: ä, ö, y. **Neutral vowels**: e, i. A simple word never mixes back and front vowels. This is **vowel harmony**, and every ending follows it.

cards.title: Which ending?
cards.body: Many endings come in two versions: `-ssa`/`-ssä` (in) and `-ko`/`-kö` (question). If the word has **a, o or u** anywhere, use the back version: `talo|ssa`. If not, use the front version: `kylä|ssä`. Words with only e and i also take the front version: `Helsingi|ssä`.

cards.title: A quick scan
cards.body: Scan the word for a, o or u. Found one? Use the ending with a or o. None? Use the ending with ä or ö. In a compound word, look at the **last part**: `kotikylä|ssä` (in the home village), because `kylä` decides.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Don't mix the groups: `kylässa` and `talossä` are mistakes every Finn notices. `olet` has an o, so `Oletko?`. `tiedät` has only ä, e and i, so `Tiedätkö?`.

terms.say: A Finnish rule: endings match the word's vowels. Words with a, o or u take endings with a or o; other words take endings with ä or ö.
a, o and u. A word with any of them takes back endings like -ssa and -ko.
ä, ö and y. Words with them, or with only e and i, take front endings like -ssä and -kö.

lessons.title: Hello and thank you
lessons.objective: Greet people, say thank you and say goodbye at any time of day.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Finnish greetings are short. `Hei` and `Moi` work almost everywhere: with friends, at work and in shops. `Hyvää päivää` (good day) is more formal. For goodbye say `Näkemiin` (polite) or `Moi moi` and `Heippa` (friendly).

cards.title: One pattern
cards.body: `Hyvää` + time of day, and the time word gets an ending: `ilta` → `iltaa`, `päivä` → `päivää`, but `yö` → `yötä` and `huomenta` (morning). Learn the four as fixed **chunks**. The ending follows vowel harmony: `iltaa` has a, `päivää` and `yötä` have ä.

cards.title: Polite words
head: Finnish
English
rows: here you are (when you give something)

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: `Mitä kuuluu?` is a real question, but the usual answer is short: `Kiitos hyvää` or `Ihan hyvää` (quite good). Nobody expects a long story. And `Moi` means hello **and** bye.

terms.say: Groups of words you learn as one piece, like Hyvää iltaa, before you know all their grammar.

lessons.title: I am, you are: olla
lessons.objective: Use the personal pronouns and all present forms of olla (to be).

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Finnish has six **personal pronouns**: `minä` (I), `sinä` (you), `hän` (he **and** she), `me` (we), `te` (you, many people or polite), `he` (they). There is no he/she difference: `hän` is for any person.

cards.title: olla (to be)
head: Person
olla
English
cards.body: ovat is the odd one out: learn it as it is.

cards.title: Drop the pronoun
cards.body: The verb ending already shows the person, so `minä`, `sinä`, `me` and `te` are often left out: `Olen Anna.` = I am Anna. `Olemme kotona.` = We are at home. Keep `hän` and `he`: `Hän on opettaja.`

cards.title: No 'a' or 'the'
cards.body: Finnish has no words for 'a' and 'the': `Hän on opettaja` = She is **a** teacher. Don't add `yksi` (one).

cards.title: Spoken vs written
cards.body: In speech you hear `mä` and `sä` for `minä` and `sinä`, and `se` (it) for people. In writing, and in the exam, use `minä`, `sinä` and `hän`.

terms.say: Short words for people: I, you, he/she, we, you (many), they. In Finnish: minä, sinä, hän, me, te, he.

lessons.title: Verb type 1: puhua, asua
lessons.objective: Use type 1 verbs (puhua, asua, ymmärtää) in the present tense for every person.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Many Finnish verbs end in two vowels: `puhua` (speak), `asua` (live), `kysyä` (ask). These are **verb type 1**. To find the **stem**, drop the last -a or -ä: `puhu-`. Then add the person ending.

cards.title: Present tense
head: Person
Ending
puhua
asua
cards.body: For hän, the stem's last vowel is doubled: puhu → puhuu.

cards.title: Already long
cards.body: If the basic form ends in -aa or -ää, the hän form looks the same: `ostaa` (buy) → `hän ostaa`. The vowel can't get any longer. The `-vat`/`-vät` ending follows vowel harmony: `puhuvat`, but `kysyvät`.

cards.title: Watch out: ymmärtää
cards.body: `ymmärtää` (understand) changes **rt → rr** in the minä, sinä, me and te forms: `ymmärrän`, `ymmärrät`, `ymmärrämme`, `ymmärrätte`. The hän and he forms keep rt: `ymmärtää`, `ymmärtävät`. `tietää` (know) works the same way: `tiedän`, but `hän tietää`. This is **consonant gradation**.

cards.title: ymmärtää (understand)
head: Person
Form
cards.body: You will meet consonant gradation properly in World 2.

terms.say: The biggest group of Finnish verbs. The basic form ends in two vowels, like puhua, asua or kysyä.
The part of a word you add endings to. For puhua the stem is puhu-.
A consonant inside a word changes when an ending is added, like rt → rr in ymmärrän or t → d in tiedän.

lessons.title: Questions with -ko/-kö
lessons.objective: Ask yes/no questions with -ko/-kö and simple questions with question words.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: To make a **yes/no question**, take the verb, add **-ko** or **-kö**, and put it first: `Sinä puhut` → `Puhutko sinä?` No extra word like 'do' is needed. The ending follows vowel harmony: `Puhutko?` but `Ymmärrätkö?`

cards.title: Saying yes
cards.body: Answer yes by repeating the verb in your own person: `Puhutko suomea?` – `Puhun.` (I do.) `Kyllä` (yes) also works. In speech you'll hear `joo`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: With a question word, **don't** add -ko: `Missä asut?`, not `Missä asutko?`. The -ko/-kö ending is only for yes/no questions.

terms.say: A question you answer with yes or no. Finnish makes it by adding -ko or -kö to the first word, usually the verb.

lessons.title: Saying no
lessons.objective: Make negative sentences with en, et, ei, emme, ette and eivät.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Finnish says 'not' with a **negative verb** that changes for the person: `en`, `et`, `ei`, `emme`, `ette`, `eivät`. The main verb loses its person ending and stays as the **stem**: `puhun` → `en puhu`.

cards.title: An easy trick
cards.body: Take the minä form and drop the -n: `puhun` → `puhu`, `asun` → `asu`, `ymmärrän` → `ymmärrä`, `olen` → `ole`. That form goes after every negative verb: `en ymmärrä`, `hän ei ymmärrä`, `he eivät ole`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Don't keep the person ending on the main verb: `en puhun` and `hän ei puhuu` are wrong. The negative verb carries the person; the main verb is only the stem: `en puhu`, `hän ei puhu`.

cards.title: Short answers
cards.body: `Ei` alone means 'no'. A fuller answer repeats the verb: `Oletko väsynyt?` (Are you tired?) – `En ole.` `Puhuuko hän ruotsia?` – `Ei puhu.`

terms.say: The Finnish word for 'not'. It changes with the person: en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät.
The part of the verb left when you drop the minä ending -n: puhun → puhu.

lessons.title: Numbers 0–100
lessons.objective: Say, write and understand numbers from 0 to 100.

cards.title: 11 to 19
cards.body: For 11–19, add **-toista** to the number: `yksitoista` (11), `kaksitoista` (12), `viisitoista` (15), `yhdeksäntoista` (19).

cards.title: Tens
cards.body: For the tens, add **-kymmentä** ('tens'): `kaksikymmentä` (20), `viisikymmentä` (50). Then add the units straight on: `kaksikymmentäyksi` (21), `neljäkymmentäseitsemän` (47). 100 is `sata`.

cards.title: One long word
cards.body: Numbers are written as one word, with no spaces: `kolmekymmentäviisi` (35). Split it in your head: kolme | kymmentä | viisi = 3 | tens | 5.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: `kahdeksan` (8) and `yhdeksän` (9) look alike: read them slowly. Phone numbers are read one digit at a time: 040 = `nolla neljä nolla`.

lessons.title: Days and time
lessons.objective: Name the days of the week, say on which day something happens and tell the time.

cards.title: Days of the week
head: Day
on that day
Day
on that day
cards.body: Days start with a small letter. Add -na for 'on': maanantaina = on Monday.

cards.title: Telling the time
cards.body: Ask `Paljonko kello on?` (What time is it?). Answer `Kello on` + number: `Kello on kolme` (It's three o'clock). `tasan` means exactly. Timetables use the 24-hour clock and the short form `klo`: `klo 18` = 6 pm.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: `puoli` looks **forward** to the next hour: `puoli kolme` is half way to three, so 2:30, not 3:30.

cards.title: Weekend
cards.body: `viikonloppu` = weekend, `viikonloppuna` = at the weekend. Same -na ending as the days.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.objective: Say your name, where you are from, where you live, what languages you speak and what you do.

items.en: I speak English and a little Finnish.

cards.title: Country: a fixed chunk
cards.body: `Olen kotoisin` + country with **-sta/-stä** = I'm from…: `Ruotsista`, `Saksasta`, `Virosta`. Learn the country forms as a **chunk** for now; this 'from' ending comes back in World 2. A few countries take -lta/-ltä instead: `Venäjältä` (from Russia).

cards.title: Countries and languages
head: Country
I'm from…
I speak…
cards.body: Countries start with a capital letter, languages with a small one.

cards.title: Languages: a fixed chunk
cards.body: After `puhua` (speak) and `ymmärtää` (understand), a language gets **-a/-ä**: `Puhun englantia`, `Ymmärrän ruotsia`. Finnish itself is a little different: `suomi` → `Puhun suomea`.

cards.title: Job and family
cards.body: Job: `Olen` + job, with no 'a': `Olen opettaja`, `Olen opiskelija`. Family as chunks: `Olen naimisissa` (I'm married), `Minulla on kaksi lasta` (I have two children). The `minulla on` pattern is explained in World 3.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Nationality and country are different words: `Olen englantilainen` (I'm English) but `Olen kotoisin Englannista` (I'm from England). Don't write the country's basic form after kotoisin: `Olen kotoisin Englanti` is wrong.

terms.say: A group of words you learn as one piece, like Olen kotoisin…, before you learn all its grammar.

lessons.title: Me and my background
lessons.objective: Understand people talking about themselves and write a short reply, using everything from this world.

cards.title: In the exam
cards.body: YKI often starts with everyday topics like **me and my background**: name, home country, languages, family, job and where you live. You may hear someone introduce themselves, or write a short message to a classmate. Use short, correct sentences you know well.

cards.title: Replying
cards.body: A good reply has three parts: greet (`Hei Ahmed!`), answer the questions, and ask one back (`Entä sinä?`, `Puhutko…?`). End in a friendly way: `Nähdään kurssilla!` (See you at the course!) and your name.

cards.title: Check before you send
cards.body: Three quick checks: the verb matches the person (`minä asun`, `hän asuu`); endings follow vowel harmony (`Puhutko`, `Ymmärrätkö`); long sounds are written double (`tuuli`, `kissa`, `mutta`).

questions.q: Which letter sounds like the 'a' in English 'cat'?
wrong: Finnish a is like the 'a' in 'father'.
ö is like the vowel in 'fur'.
questions.explain: ä is its own letter: the open front vowel of 'cat'. It is not a decorated a.

wrong: Finnish j is never the English 'j' sound.
That would be the letter h.
Finnish has no 'sh' sound in ja.
questions.explain: Finnish j sounds like English y, so ja is said 'ya'.

questions.q: Where is the stress in Finnish words?
options: It changes from word to word
wrong: Length and stress are separate in Finnish.
Finnish stress is fixed, which makes reading easy.
questions.explain: Finnish main stress is always on the first syllable: HEL-sin-ki, SUO-mi.

questions.audio: Hei! Tämä on Yrjö. Hän on opettaja.
wrong: Jyrki starts with j (a 'y' sound) and ends in i. The name you heard starts with the vowel y and ends in ö.
Urho starts with u, a back vowel, not y.
Jouko has the glide ou, not ö.
questions.explain: Yrjö starts with the vowel y (round-lipped 'ee') and ends with ö.

questions.hint: Do you speak Finnish? – Yes, a little. Use y and ä.
questions.explain: kyllä (yes) is written with y and ä. Without the dots it is not a word.
Good night is Hyvää yötä. yö has the glide yö, and the ending -tä has ä because y and ö are front vowels.

wrong: Fire is tuli, with a short u.
Customs is tulli, with a double l.
questions.explain: tuuli has a long uu and means wind. tuli (fire) and tulli (customs) differ only in length.

wrong: kissa has a, so the end stays a: kissä isn't a word.
kisaa is a form of kisa (contest).
questions.explain: Cat is kissa: double ss, held a moment longer. One s gives kisa, contest.

wrong: Fire is tuli, with a short u. The speaker held the u: tuuli.
Rug is matto; it isn't mentioned.
questions.explain: tuuli (long uu) means wind. Tuuli on kova = the wind is strong.

questions.q: Kuka? No, I mean the flower: ___ (flower)
questions.hint: flower = kuka with a double consonant
questions.explain: kukka (flower) has a double kk. kuka with one k means who.

questions.hint: The cat is at home. Double s.
questions.explain: Cat is kissa with a double ss. kisa would mean contest.

questions.hint: I speak English but not Finnish. muta = mud
questions.explain: but = mutta, with a double tt. With one t, muta means mud.

wrong: talo has a and o, so the ending must be -ssa, not -ssä.
The 'in' ending has a double s: -ssa.
questions.explain: Vowel harmony: talo has back vowels (a, o), so it takes -ssa: talossa.

wrong: puhut has u, so it takes -ko: Puhutko?
ymmärrät has only y and ä (front vowels), so it takes -kö: Ymmärrätkö?
asut has a and u, so it takes -ko: Asutko?
questions.explain: olet has an o (a back vowel), so the question ending is -ko: Oletko?

questions.audio: Minä asun kylässä. Kylä on pieni.
wrong: A house is talo (talossa); you heard kylässä.
The place is small: Kylä on pieni.
questions.explain: kylässä = in a village. The ending -ssä has ä because kylä has front vowels.
talo has a and o (back vowels), so the ending is -ssa: talo|ssa.
kylä has y and ä (front vowels), so the ending is -ssä: kylä|ssä.
puhut has u, a back vowel, so it takes -ko: Puhutko?
ymmärrät has only y and ä (front vowels), so it takes -kö: Ymmärrätkö?

questions.q: It's 8 in the morning and you meet your neighbour. What do you say?
questions.explain: Hyvää huomenta = good morning. Hyvää + time of day is the pattern.

questions.q: You hand a colleague a cup of coffee. What do you say?
wrong: Kiitos = thank you; that's what your colleague says.
questions.explain: Ole hyvä is said when you give something: 'here you are'.

questions.audio: Hei Liisa! Mitä kuuluu? – Kiitos hyvää. Entä sinulle?
questions.explain: Kiitos hyvää = fine, thanks. Entä sinulle? = and you?
Hyvää + time of day: ilta → iltaa. ilta has a, so the ending is -a.
päivä → päivää. päivä has ä, so the ending is -ä (vowel harmony).

questions.q: Mitä kuuluu? – ___ hyvää. Entä sinulle? (thank you)
questions.hint: How are you? – Fine, thanks. And you?
questions.explain: The usual short answer is Kiitos hyvää: 'thanks, fine'.
Mitä (sinulle) kuuluu? is the fixed greeting question. sinulle (to you) can sit before or after kuuluu.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “Good day and welcome!”
questions.explain: Hyvää päivää is one chunk; ja (and) links it to tervetuloa (welcome).
olla with minä: olen. The -n ending means 'I'.
olla with hän (he/she): on.
olla with me (we): olemme. The -mme ending means 'we'.
olla with he (they): ovat. It's the irregular form of olla.
olla with te (you, many): olette. The -tte ending means 'you (plural)'.
sinä (you, one person) goes with olet. The -t ending means 'you'.

wrong: se means 'it'. Finns say it about people in speech, but not in writing.
questions.explain: hän is used for any person, man or woman.

questions.audio: Tämä on Mikko. Hän on opettaja. Minä olen opiskelija.
wrong: That's the speaker: Minä olen opiskelija.
questions.explain: Hän on opettaja = he is a teacher. hän refers to Mikko.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “She is a doctor.”
questions.explain: Subject + olla + job. No word for 'a' is needed.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “We are at home.”
questions.explain: me (we) + olemme. kotona = at home.
Verb type 1: stem puhu- + -n for minä: puhun.
For hän, double the stem's last vowel: asu- → asuu.
Stem puhu- + -mme for me: puhumme.
ymmärtää changes rt → rr in the minä form: ymmärrän (consonant gradation).
Stem asu- + -vat for he (they): asuvat. asua has a and u, so -vat, not -vät.

questions.q: Which form fits? Sinä ___ hyvin englantia.
wrong: puhutte is the te (you, many) form.
questions.explain: sinä takes the -t ending: puhut. Sinä puhut hyvin englantia = you speak English well.

wrong: The hän form keeps rt; rr is only in minä, sinä, me and te forms.
That's only the stem; hän needs the long vowel.
questions.explain: The hän form of ymmärtää keeps the strong rt and looks like the basic form: hän ymmärtää.

questions.audio: Minä olen Lena. Asun Espoossa. Puhun saksaa ja englantia.
wrong: Finnish would be suomea; she said englantia.
questions.explain: Puhun saksaa ja englantia = I speak German and English.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “They live in Tampere.”
questions.explain: he (they) + asuvat. Subject, verb, then the place.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I speak a little Finnish.”
questions.explain: Puhun already means 'I speak'. vähän (a little) usually comes before the language.

questions.hint: Do you speak Finnish? sinä form + -ko/-kö
questions.explain: sinä form puhut + -ko (u is a back vowel): Puhutko? The verb comes first.

questions.hint: Are you a student? sinä form + -ko/-kö
questions.explain: olet + -ko: Oletko? olet has o, so the ending is -ko.

questions.hint: Does she live in Vantaa? hän form + -ko/-kö
questions.explain: hän form asuu + -ko: Asuuko? a and u are back vowels.

questions.hint: Do you (all) understand English? te form + -ko/-kö
questions.explain: te form ymmärrätte (rt → rr) + -kö, because the word has only front and neutral vowels: Ymmärrättekö?

wrong: With a question word, don't add -ko.
questions.explain: Question word + verb: Missä sinä asut? -ko/-kö is only for yes/no questions.

wrong: ovat has o and a, so it takes -ko, not -kö.
questions.explain: he (they) + ovat, and the question ending -ko: Ovatko he kotona?

questions.audio: Hei! Oletko sinä Sara? Minä olen Leo. Asutko sinä Espoossa?
wrong: He asks this second, and only as a yes/no question: Asutko Espoossa?
He doesn't ask about the time.
questions.explain: Oletko sinä Sara? = Are you Sara? olet + -ko makes a yes/no question.

questions.q: Build the question: “Do you speak English?”
questions.explain: The verb with -ko comes first, then the subject and the language.

questions.q: Build the question: “Where are you from?”
questions.explain: Question word first: Mistä (from where) + sinä olet + kotoisin. No -ko with a question word.
The negative verb for minä is en. The main verb stays as the stem: en puhu.
After a negative verb, olla is ole: olen minus -n. Hän ei ole.
The negative verb for he (they) is eivät. asu stays as the stem.
Take the minä form ymmärrän and drop -n: en ymmärrä. The rr stays.

wrong: The main verb loses its -n after en: puhu.
ei is for hän; minä needs en.
puhuu is the hän form; after en use the stem puhu.
questions.explain: minä → en, and the main verb is the stem: Minä en puhu saksaa.

questions.q: *Oletko sinä opettaja?* Which answer means “No, I'm not.”?
questions.explain: You answer about yourself, so use en: En ole.

questions.audio: Minä olen Tom. Puhun englantia. En puhu suomea, mutta ymmärrän vähän.
wrong: En puhu suomea = he doesn't speak Finnish.
He says ymmärrän vähän: I understand a little.
questions.explain: En puhu suomea, mutta ymmärrän vähän = I don't speak Finnish, but I understand a little.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “We don't live in Espoo.”
questions.explain: me + emme (negative for we) + the stem asu.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “She isn't a teacher.”
questions.explain: hän + ei + ole (the stem of olla) + job.
7 = seitsemän. It ends in -än with ä.
11–19 = number + -toista: viisi + toista = viisitoista, one word.

questions.hint: I am 32 years old. One word.
questions.explain: kolme + kymmentä (3 tens) + kaksi, written as one word: kolmekymmentäkaksi.
kahdeksan (8) + kymmentä (tens) = 80.

questions.q: How do you write 47 in Finnish?
questions.explain: Tens first, then units: neljä + kymmentä + seitsemän = 47.

questions.audio: Puhelinnumero on nolla neljä viisi, kolme kuusi kahdeksan, yhdeksän nolla yksi.
questions.q: Which phone number do you hear?
wrong: You heard neljä (4) before viisi (5): 045, not 054.
The end is yhdeksän nolla yksi: 901.
questions.explain: Phone numbers are read digit by digit: nolla neljä viisi = 045.

wrong: 20 is only kaksikymmentä; you also heard kolme.
questions.explain: kaksikymmentä (20) + kolme (3) = 23.
'On' a day: add -na. maanantai → maanantaina. Small first letter.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Days of the week

questions.hint: I'm not at work on Friday.
questions.explain: perjantai + -na = perjantaina (on Friday). The negative is en + ole.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Days of the week

questions.explain: puoli looks forward to the next hour: puoli kolme = half way to three = 2:30.

questions.q: *Kello on puoli viisi.* What time is it?
wrong: puoli looks forward: half way to five, not after five.
questions.explain: puoli viisi = half way to five = 4:30.

questions.q: Read the note: *Suomen kurssi tiistaina ja torstaina klo 17–19.* When is the course?
wrong: maanantai is Monday and keskiviikko Wednesday; the note says tiistaina ja torstaina.
klo 17–19 is 5–7 pm on the 24-hour clock.
Friday is perjantai; the note says torstaina (Thursday).
questions.explain: tiistaina = on Tuesday, torstaina = on Thursday, klo 17–19 = 5–7 pm.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Days of the week

questions.audio: Tänään on keskiviikko. Suomen kurssi on huomenna kello kuusi.
wrong: Today is Wednesday, but the course is huomenna (tomorrow).
questions.explain: Today is keskiviikko (Wednesday), so huomenna (tomorrow) is Thursday. kello kuusi = six o'clock.
Tänään (today) + on + the day in its basic form.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Days of the week

questions.explain: Olen kotoisin + country with -sta/-stä: Ruotsi → Ruotsista (o and u are back vowels, so -sta).

questions.hint: I speak English and a little Finnish.
questions.explain: After puhua the language gets -a/-ä. suomi changes its last vowel: suomea.
The chunk Olen kotoisin + country with -sta: Englannista.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I live in Espoo and I speak German.”
questions.explain: Two short sentences joined with ja (and): Asun Espoossa + puhun saksaa.

questions.audio: Hei! Olen Maria. Olen kotoisin Espanjasta. Asun nyt Turussa. Olen opiskelija.
wrong: Espanjasta = from Spain: that's where she comes from.
questions.explain: Asun nyt Turussa = I live in Turku now. Olen kotoisin Espanjasta = I'm from Spain.

questions.q: Which sentence means *I am English* (my nationality)?
wrong: After kotoisin the country needs -sta: Englannista. And this is about the country, not nationality.
questions.explain: Nationality: Olen englantilainen. Country: Olen kotoisin Englannista.
Ahmed is one person (hän), so the stem's vowel doubles: asuu.
After en the verb is the stem: puhun minus -n = puhu.

questions.q: Build the reply: “I don't speak Arabic, but I speak English.”
answer: En puhu arabiaa, mutta puhun englantia
questions.explain: Negative part first (en + stem puhu), then mutta (but) and the positive form puhun. A comma goes before mutta.

questions.audio: Hei! Minä olen Ahmed. Olen kotoisin Irakista, mutta asun nyt Vantaalla. Olen bussinkuljettaja. Puhun arabiaa ja englantia.
questions.explain: Olen bussinkuljettaja = I'm a bus driver (bussi + kuljettaja, driver).

questions.audio: Moi! Minä olen Kati. Olen opettaja. Olen töissä maanantaina ja keskiviikkona. Kurssi alkaa kello viisi.
questions.q: On which days does Kati work?
wrong: Those would be tiistaina ja torstaina.
Tuesday is tiistai; she said keskiviikkona (Wednesday).
Friday is perjantai; she said maanantaina (Monday).
questions.explain: maanantaina = on Monday, keskiviikkona = on Wednesday.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Days of the week

writing.title: Introduce yourself
writing.situation: You start a Finnish course. The teacher asks everyone to write a short message to the group. Introduce yourself.
writing.model: Hei kaikki! Minä olen Sam. Olen kotoisin Englannista, mutta asun nyt Tampereella. Olen sairaanhoitaja. Puhun englantia ja vähän ranskaa. Ymmärrän vähän suomea. Hauska tutustua! Terveisin Sam
checklist: I started with a greeting (Hei kaikki!)
Verbs match the person (minä olen, minä asun, minä puhun)
I ended with a closing and my name

writing.title: Reply to a classmate
writing.situation: Your classmate Ahmed writes to you: “Hei! Olen Ahmed. Olen kotoisin Irakista ja asun Vantaalla. Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? Puhutko arabiaa?” Write a short reply.
writing.model: Hei Ahmed! Minä olen Lin. Olen kotoisin Kiinasta. En puhu arabiaa, mutta puhun kiinaa ja englantia. Asun Helsingissä. Puhutko sinä englantia? Nähdään kurssilla! Lin
checklist: I answered both of his questions
I used en + stem for 'no' (en puhu)
I asked him a question with -ko/-kö
I ended with a closing (Nähdään kurssilla!) and my name
